## Concept Overview Virtual DOM is a JavaScript representation of the real DOM that enables efficient updates through diffing and reconciliation. React creates a new VDOM tree on each render, compares it with the previous tree, and calculates the minimal changes needed. ## Implementation ```jsx // Without keys - inefficient re-renders function BadList({ items }) { return items.map(item =>
  • {item.name}
    • ); } // With keys - optimized updates function GoodList({ items }) { return items.map(item =>
  • {item.name}
    • ); } ``` **Diffing Algorithm Rules:** - Different element types → replace entire subtree - Same element type → update attributes only - Lists → use keys to match elements ## Trade-offs **Pros:** - Batched DOM updates improve performance - Declarative programming model - Cross-browser compatibility **Cons:** - Memory overhead for VDOM trees - Initial render slower than direct DOM manipulation - Not optimal for frequent small updates ## Common Pitfalls - Using array indices as keys for mutable lists - Missing keys in dynamic lists causing unnecessary re-renders - Unstable keys causing component state loss - Over-relying on VDOM for performance-critical animations

questions.explanation:
To implement optimistic updates with useReducer, I'd create a reducer that handles three action types: optimistic updates (immediate UI changes), success responses (confirm updates), and failure responses (rollbacks). The reducer state would include both the optimistic state and a pending operations queue to track in-flight requests. For example, when liking a post, dispatch an 'OPTIMISTIC_LIKE' action that immediately updates the UI and adds the operation to the pending queue, then handle the server response with either 'LIKE_SUCCESS' or 'LIKE_FAILURE' actions.

The middleware layer would intercept actions to implement request deduplication using a Map of pending operations keyed by resource ID and operation type, preventing duplicate requests. It would also maintain operation sequencing through a queue that ensures subsequent operations for the same resource wait for pending operations to complete. Race conditions are mitigated by timestamping each operation and rejecting stale responses, while UI consistency is maintained through atomic state updates and proper error boundaries to handle rollback scenarios gracefully.

questions.explanation: The solution involves creating a custom hook, let's call it `useSmartState`, that automatically detects whether a component should use local or global state. This hook would first check if the component is wrapped in a specific context provider that indicates shared state usage. If the provider is present, it would connect to a global store (possibly using Zustand, Jotai, or a custom implementation with useReducer and subscriptions). If no provider is found, it would fall back to regular useState for local component state. The global store would implement a subscription pattern where components only re-render when the specific state slice they depend on changes, using selectors similar to Redux's useSelector. To make the transition seamless, you'd implement a context provider that can be conditionally applied at different levels of the component tree, allowing the same component to work in both local and global scenarios without code changes.
